    • What this means for SAT: The “no asymptotically stable >3‑quark states” heuristic remains viable; if SAT predicts quasi‑stable composites, their lifetimes must be reconciled with measured widths.

    • No observation; mode‑dependent limits now push lifetimes beyond 10^34 yr in several channels.

# SAT<sub>4D</sub> Predictions vs. Observational Constraints

## Prediction A: θ₄-Defect Induced Achromatic Phase Steps

### Validation
SAT<sub>4D</sub> predicts that crossing a topological θ₄-defect induces a fixed, wavelength-independent phase shift (Δφ) in electromagnetic waves, proportional to the defect’s net charge (Δφ = κ·2πN, for integer *N*). Observationally, no robust evidence of such achromatic phase steps has been reported yet, which is consistent with the prediction *if* such defects are rare or produce only small effects. Current cosmological polarization measurements limit any isotropic, wavelength-independent rotation of light to ≲0.3°【18†L56-L63】. This effectively means that large, ubiquitous phase offsets (on the order of tens of degrees or more) are *not* present across the sky – a finding that does not contradict SAT<sub>4D</sub> so long as any θ₄-induced phase shifts are either much smaller in magnitude or confined to localized regions (e.g. only near occasional defects)【18†L57-L64】. In other words, the absence of a large global polarization rotation is compatible with the SAT<sub>4D</sub> scenario, which would posit only discrete jumps at defect boundaries (potentially very sparse in the observable Universe). Laboratory optics experiments have likewise not seen any unexplained quantized, achromatic phase jumps, again indicating that if the θ₄-defect effect exists, it lies below current detection thresholds in controlled settings.

### Contradictions
Any *broad* or significant achromatic phase rotation across astronomical sources would conflict with existing bounds. For example, a prediction of an order-unity phase jump (say Δφ ~ 0.24 rad ≈ 14°) everywhere in the sky would be decisively falsified – such a large, fixed rotation is ruled out as a global phenomenon by CMB polarization data【18†L56-L63】. The evidence map explicitly notes that observations of frequency-independent optical phase shifts at ≫degree scales *“conflict with current EM bounds unless highly localized/rare”*【18†L57-L64】. Thus, SAT<sub>4D</sub> must avoid predicting an all-sky effect of that magnitude. So far there are no “red-flag” inconsistencies: the null detection of large achromatic birefringence simply constrains the defect density and strength (e.g. defects, if they exist, must be few and/or κ·N must be relatively small). A single pronounced violation – for instance, if some interferometric or polarization observation found a sudden, path-independent phase jump where none of the known physics can produce it – would serve as a falsification. No such decisive counterexample has been seen to date. In summary, the lack of widespread achromatic phase steps is in **tension** only with any SAT model that would predict them to be common or large; fortunately, the θ₄-defect idea as stated can remain viable by asserting that any effects are subtle or rare, which current observations permit.

### Outlook
This prediction offers crisp experimental tests in both astrophysical and laboratory contexts. On the cosmic side, upcoming CMB polarization surveys and deep optical/radio polarization catalogs will improve sensitivity to tiny rotations. If a θ₄-induced step exists, it might be detected as a consistent offset in polarization angle for sources straddling a certain boundary on the sky. Future analyses could look for patchy, quantized rotation angles – e.g. multiple of some baseline Δφ – which would be a telltale sign of topological domain boundaries. Even a localized detection of a wavelength-independent phase step (for example, light from a quasar pair showing a relative phase difference that is identical across optical bands) would support this SAT<sub>4D</sub> effect. As measurements push below the 0.1° level in polarization rotation uncertainty, they will either discover subtle signals of θ₄-defects or further constrain κ·N (forcing N=1 defects to have very small coupling κ, or N to be extremely rare). On the laboratory side, precision interferometers or cavity experiments might attempt to simulate or detect a θ₄-like misalignment – for instance, using metamaterials or novel optical paths to mimic a 4D defect crossing. While challenging, such tests could soon reach the sensitivity to observe minute, quantized phase shifts independent of wavelength. In short, improved coverage and resolution (e.g. the next generation of CMB polarization maps, or high-contrast interferometry) will either lend support by catching a rare phase jump event or tighten the noose by eliminating the remaining parameter space for θ₄-optical interactions. SAT researchers are already encouraged to frame any large predicted rotation as *localized* effects【18†L57-L64】, and this will become an increasingly testable claim in the near future.

## Prediction B: Gravitational Wave Polarization from Filament Anisotropy

### Validation
The SAT<sub>4D</sub> framework introduces a small dimensionless anisotropy parameter (ε) associated with filament orientations, which in a “toy” model yields a fraction of gravitational-wave (GW) power in scalar and vector polarizations: *f*<sub>scalar</sub> ≈ c<sub>S</sub>·ε² and *f*<sub>vector</sub> ≈ c<sub>V</sub>·ε² (with the dominant tensor mode fraction *f*<sub>tensor</sub> ≈ 1 – O(ε²)【1†L49-L57】). This means that if ε is very small, the non-tensor polarization components would be correspondingly tiny. Current observations are fully consistent with this scenario — in fact, they have so far revealed *no* appreciable deviation from General Relativity’s purely tensor GWs. LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA data (through GWTC-3) show no evidence of scalar or vector GW polarizations in the ~10–1000 Hz band【18†L26-L34】, which implies that any *f*<sub>scalar</sub>, *f*<sub>vector</sub> must lie below the detectors’ sensitivity. This aligns with the SAT<sub>4D</sub> expectation provided ε is sufficiently small (or c<sub>S>, c<sub>V</sub> are small): the theory does not predict a large signal that should have been seen already, only a subtle effect at the edge of detectability. Likewise, pulsar timing arrays observing the nanohertz GW background have reported Hellings–Downs spatial correlations consistent with a standard (tensor) stochastic background【18†L39-L47】. The absence of odd correlation patterns (which would indicate alternative polarizations) is again consistent with SAT’s compatibility with GR in the limit of tiny ε. In summary, the observational stance is *compatibility*: the predicted scaling of extra polarization modes is not supported by any positive evidence yet, but it also isn’t refuted — it remains plausible in the small-ε regime allowed by current data【18†L26-L32】.

### Contradictions
A serious contradiction would arise if SAT<sub>4D</sub> required a substantial fraction of GWs to be in scalar/vector form in regimes already well-tested. For example, were the theory to predict *f*<sub>scalar+vector</sub> ~ 0.5 for LIGO-frequency waves, it would be flatly inconsistent with the observations (which show no such large deviations in waveforms or polarization patterns). In reality, the non-detections so far act as **constraints** rather than outright falsification: they bound ε (and the coupling constants c<sub>S</sub>, c<sub>V</sub>) from above. Quantitatively, advanced LIGO analyses have placed 95% confidence limits on the energy densities of alternative polarization modes in the stochastic background on the order of Ω<sub>scalar</sub> < 1×10^-7 and Ω<sub>vector</sub> < 10^-7 relative to the total【11†L19-L27】. These stringent bounds imply that ε² (times order-unity coefficients) must be ≲10^-7 in the present universe’s GW background, or else such extra polarizations would have been detected. The evidence map concurs, noting that any model with extra GW polarizations must keep their excitation **“sufficiently small in LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA bands, or confine them to other regimes”**【18†L26-L32】. Thus, if a particular SAT<sub>4D</sub> realization had predicted, say, a 5–10% scalar polarization component in ordinary binary black hole mergers, we would consider it essentially falsified by existing data (a clear red flag). At this time no blatant conflict has emerged — the theory can accommodate the null results by tuning ε small — but the **lack** of any hint of non-tensor modes forces SAT to a rather unexciting corner of parameter space. Should future observations continue to show purely tensor GWs even as sensitivity improves dramatically, it would tighten the squeeze. Conversely, if SAT cannot naturally explain why ε is so tiny (without fine-tuning), that theoretical issue might also undermine it. In short, *current* observations impose that SAT’s GW anisotropy effect be very weak; any prediction to the contrary is already ruled out【18†L26-L34】.

### Outlook
The coming years will markedly improve our ability to detect or constrain small GW polarization effects, providing a critical test of this SAT<sub>4D</sub> prediction. As the global network of interferometers expands (with LIGO-India, improved KAGRA, and eventually next-generation detectors like Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope), polarization separation will become more precise. Even a percent-level contribution of scalar or vector modes in compact binary signals could be picked out by careful analysis of detector patterns and cross-correlations. If the filament anisotropy mechanism is correct, one intriguing possibility is that certain classes of sources (e.g. binary mergers aligned with large-scale cosmic filaments or anisotropic environments) might show a small but systematic departure from purely tensor polarization. Detecting such a trend would be a major victory for SAT<sub>4D</sub>. On the other hand, continuing null results will push the admissible ε to ever smaller values, perhaps approaching the point where SAT<sub>4D</sub> would need to justify why ε is nonzero yet vanishingly small. Pulsar Timing Array efforts (NANOGrav, IPTA, etc.) will also advance: with more pulsars and longer baselines, they could search for non-Einsteinian correlation signatures (monopolar or dipolar correlations in the GW background) as a sign of scalar or vector modes. So far the PTA data match the textbook GR expectation【18†L39-L47】, but improved statistics may reveal sub-dominant components — for example, a small dipole term superposed on the Hellings–Downs curve would indicate a scalar “breathing” mode presence. Additionally, space-based GW observatories like LISA will probe entirely new frequency bands; if SAT’s extra polarization effect grows with wavelength or source scale, LISA might have a better chance of seeing it. In summary, the prediction of GW polarization mixing is entering a testable regime: either subtle signals will emerge as instruments improve (validating the SAT anisotropy with measured *f*<sub>scalar,vector</sub> vs. ε relationships), or continued absence of detection will further constrain or potentially refute the idea. Notably, the evidence map suggests that **any** significant detection of non-tensor polarizations in coming data would *immediately* elevate the need for a SAT-like mechanism【18†L102-L107】, which means this aspect of SAT<sub>4D</sub> could move from speculative to essential if observational fortunes change.

## Prediction C: Exotic Hadron Width Ordering via Topological Reconnection

### Validation
SAT<sub>4D</sub> predicts a strict ordering in the decay widths of exotic multiquark hadrons based on their topological linkage complexity. In essence, a state with more constituent quarks (higher *n*) cannot have a *narrower* (longer-lived) width than a similar state with fewer constituents, given the same environmental conditions. This arises because each additional parton linkage is assumed to introduce an extra “reconnection” barrier to decay, so more complex exotics face at least as large a decay rate as simpler ones【1†L73-L78】【1†L65-L72】. Current experimental findings are **consistent** with this pattern. Multiple exotic hadrons have been observed (especially by LHCb and other experiments), including tetraquarks (4-quark states like the T_cc^+) and pentaquarks (5-quark states), and all of them are resonances with finite (often sizable) decay widths【18†L75-L82】. Crucially, none of these states is anywhere near stable on nuclear timescales – all decay rapidly via strong or electromagnetic interactions. For example, the recently discovered T_cc^+ (a $cc\bar{u}\bar{d}$ tetraquark) is “narrow” in the sense of a small width (~50 keV) compared to typical hadron resonances, yet even this corresponds to an extremely short lifetime (~10^−23 s) and it decays promptly【18†L75-L82】. The observed pentaquarks (such as the $P_c$ states) have widths on the order of a few MeV (e.g. 5–20 MeV), which, as expected, are not narrower than the tetraquark widths in the same regime (indeed, pentaquarks appear at least as short-lived as, if not shorter-lived than, the tetraquark states)【18†L75-L82】. Moreover, no “exotic” beyond pentaquarks (like hypothetical hexaquarks or higher) has been confirmed – and certainly none that is long-lived. This all aligns with the SAT<sub>4D</sub> heuristic that more elaborate multiquark configurations are disfavored from having long lifetimes. The general empirical rule that there are **“no asymptotically stable >3-quark states”** remains unbroken【18†L75-L82】, which is exactly in line with SAT’s expectations. In summary, the available evidence supports the SAT<sub>4D</sub> width-ordering: higher-$n$ exotics decay at least as readily as lower-$n$ ones, and none have shown anomalously long lifetimes that would violate the predicted ordering.

### Contradictions
To date, no experimental observation has blatantly contradicted this prediction. A decisive falsification would require finding an exotic hadron that is significantly more stable than a simpler counterpart – for instance, a pentaquark with a much narrower width than some well-established tetraquark under similar conditions, or the discovery of a hexaquark that is essentially stable (e.g. does not decay on measurable timescales). No such discovery has been made. In fact, the community has *not* seen any exotic multiquark state that lives beyond a microsecond, let alone one that could challenge ordinary nuclei in stability. The evidence map underscores this point with a cautionary hook: **“Detecting long-lived (> ns) tetra/pentaquarks at colliders → strains the ‘no stable exotics’ motif.”**【18†L99-L106】. In other words, if an experiment were to find a multiquark hadron that persisted for nanoseconds or longer (something that would imply a tremendously narrower width than any currently known resonance), it would pose a serious problem for SAT<sub>4D</sub>. As of 2025, nothing of the sort has been reported. Even the “narrow” T_cc^+ decays within ~10^−23 seconds, and speculative states like the H-dibaryon (a proposed 6-quark uuddss bound state) have never been observed as stable or even quasi-stable. Thus, there are no red-flag inconsistencies yet – the prediction that higher-n exotics are short-lived holds across all known cases. It should be noted that one must compare like with like: certain kinematic or channel differences can affect widths (for example, a state right at a decay threshold can appear unnaturally narrow due to limited phase space). SAT’s claim applies when comparing states in the same dynamical regime. So far, when this is accounted for, no violation of the monotonic width trend has emerged. However, if in the future an exception were found – say a pentaquark decaying purely weakly or electromagnetically while a comparable tetraquark decays strongly – yielding a pentaquark lifetime much longer – that would challenge the letter of the SAT<sub>4D</sub> prediction (or at least force a re-examination of what constitutes the “same regime”). In summary, **no contradiction at present**: all multiquark candidates fit the expectation that additional quarks do not lead to longer lifetimes, and the first sign of a stable or unusually long-lived exotic would be a clear alarm bell for SAT.

### Outlook
The ongoing and upcoming experimental programs in hadron spectroscopy will vigorously test this width-ordering prediction in finer detail. LHCb, Belle II, BES III, and future facilities will continue to discover new exotic hadrons (potentially including higher-order multiquark states such as hexaquarks or bound states of baryons like dibaryons). Each new state will offer a chance to check SAT<sub>4D</sub>’s ordering rule. **Near-term testability:** If a hexaquark or another pentaquark is observed, measuring its decay width relative to known exotics will be crucial. According to SAT<sub>4D</sub>, a hexaquark (6 quarks) should have at least as large a width as a pentaquark, all else being equal – it would be suspicious if we found a hexaquark that is significantly more long-lived than the pentaquark family. Upcoming higher-statistics runs at the LHC and future colliders will improve the precision on these widths (e.g. turning a “seen” narrow state into a well-measured width with error bars), allowing more stringent comparisons. Furthermore, novel search channels (like looking for exotic multiquark production in heavy-ion collisions or in decays of heavy particles) could reveal if any exotic states have unusually suppressed decays. If experiments confirm a molecular interpretation for some pentaquarks (as some models suggest) and yet find them short-lived, that still is fine for SAT. But if a molecular hexaquark were stable (e.g. a deuteron analog with exotic content), one might argue it evades the topological “reconnection” counting (since it’s two bound baryons). Such subtleties mean SAT<sub>4D</sub> will need to clearly define its domain of applicability. In any case, the next generation of data will either continue to uphold the no-stable-exotics rule – which would strengthen confidence in SAT<sub>4D</sub> (especially if accompanied by the predicted exponential scaling of width ratios between, say, tetra and penta states) – or uncover an unexpected long-lived multiquark that forces a revision of the theory. ## Prediction D: Mass Hierarchies from Topological Complexity

### Validation
This SAT<sub>4D</sub> prediction posits that the mass spectrum of particles (or composite states) can be understood as geometric sequences resulting from their topological complexity. Quantitatively, one assumes an exponential relation *m = m₀ · exp(-σ K)*, where *K* is an integer-like topological complexity measure (such as a count of twists or crossings in a filament) and σ is a positive constant characteristic of that class of particles【1†L85-L93】. If members of a particle family have K values in arithmetic progression (K, K+ΔK, K+2ΔK, …), their masses should form a geometric progression: m<sub>j+1</sub>/m<sub>j</sub> = exp(-σ ΔK) = constant【1†L87-L95】【1†L95-L100】. How does this stack up against real-world data? At present, no clear instance of a *perfect* geometric progression in known particle masses has been identified, but hierarchical patterns do exist broadly in nature. For example, the masses of the three charged leptons (e, μ, τ) increase dramatically from one generation to the next, and quark masses and neutrino masses show large hierarchies as well. The SAT<sub>4D</sub> ansatz provides a possible organizing principle for these: it would attribute the huge mass ratio between, say, the electron and the tau (m<sub>τ</sub>/m<sub>e</sub> ~ 3500) to a difference in topological complexity (ΔK) between those particles. In the absence of a concrete assignment of K for elementary leptons in SAT, we cannot yet check if log(mass) vs K is exactly linear, but the very existence of mass hierarchies in the Standard Model is qualitatively consistent with the idea that something (potentially topology) is responsible for exponential mass suppression. Importantly, this framework is flexible: by adjusting σ and the step ΔK, a wide range of ratios can be fitted. For instance, the extreme lightness of neutrinos (with m(νₑ) < 0.45 eV at 90% CL【18†L91-L98】) relative to, say, the top quark (~173 GeV) could be explained by a much larger effective K or a different sector parameter σ, yielding a huge suppression factor without contradicting any known bounds. In short, **there is as yet no direct experimental confirmation of masses falling in exact geometric ratios tied to a topological quantum number**, but neither is there evidence that fundamentally disfavors this notion – it remains a plausible interpretation framework for existing hierarchies. We do see approximate regularities in certain hadronic Regge trajectories and nuclear binding energy patterns, but those follow different formulas. The SAT<sub>4D</sub> approach is novel in that it predicts strict proportionality on a log scale; this is an open hypothesis that awaits dedicated testing once specific K values can be assigned to physical states.

### Contradictions
Given that the topological mass hierarchy proposal is still quite qualitative, it hasn’t yet been confronted with a smoking-gun contradiction. However, if taken literally, one might expect to already see hints of geometric scaling in known spectra – and that is not obviously the case. For example, consider the baryon octet or decuplet masses, or the spectrum of light mesons: their masses do not neatly form constant ratios; instead they follow more linear or quadratic patterns (as with Regge trajectories). The charged lepton trio (e, μ, τ) certainly do not exhibit a constant mass multiplication factor from one to the next (μ/e ≈ 207, τ/μ ≈ 17, which are very different). If SAT<sub>4D</sub> insisted on a single ΔK for those and a single σ, it would predict a fixed ratio, which is clearly not observed – a naive application would be *falsified*. Fortunately, the theory allows some flexibility: different families can have different ΔK, or additional interactions can perturb the masses【1†L95-L100】. The SAT internal notes explicitly acknowledge that *“deviations [from a perfect geometric progression] flag either K misassignment or additional SAT interactions (e.g., ψ–τ couplings)”*【1†L95-L100】. In practice, this means that if we try to fit a family’s masses to a straight line in log(m) vs K and it doesn’t work, one shouldn’t immediately throw out the theory – one might have simply identified K incorrectly or omitted some coupling. Thus, no current measurement singularly invalidates the concept; rather, the concept has yet to be sharpened to the point of making a binary pass/fail prediction. The risk of contradiction will increase once SAT<sub>4D</sub> provides a concrete mapping of particles to (K, m) pairs. At that stage, a clear outlier – e.g. a particle that should, according to its K, lie on a geometric sequence but is off by orders of magnitude – would pose a serious challenge. Another potential red flag would be if experiments discover a series of states that *should* have equal ΔK steps (perhaps a sequence of exotic hadrons distinguished by one extra knot in a flux tube each) and their masses do **not** exhibit a constant ratio. If, for instance, a set of topologically related resonances showed a broken or random pattern in mass, that would directly contradict the prediction. So far, however, we do not have such a clear experimental scenario. Even the neutrino sector, which could have been a deal-breaker if neutrino masses were degenerate or inexplicably tiny without structure, is not a contradiction per se – SAT can attribute neutrinos’ tiny masses to large K or small σ in that sector, consistent with the requirement that any mass-generation mechanism produce sub-eV neutrinos【18†L91-L98】. In summary, the absence of a simple geometric pattern in the known spectra is a point to note, but not a definitive falsification given the theory’s current malleability. The true test (and chance for contradiction) will come when SAT<sub>4D</sub> moves from the idea phase to making numeric predictions for specific series of masses.

### Outlook
The path forward for testing this prediction lies in identifying *families* of particles or states where a topological quantum number can be clearly assigned, and then checking the linear-log relation. One promising area is in hadronic physics: if SAT<sub>4D</sub> applies to QCD bound states, one could imagine classifying certain resonances by their “filament writhe/twist” (perhaps related to how gluon flux tubes knot for exotic hadrons). As experimentalists map out the spectrum of exotic hadrons (tetraquark, pentaquark, hexaquark candidates, etc.), one might see a pattern emerge in their masses. For instance, if a series of multiquark states differing by one unit of some topological count are found, plotting their masses on a log scale vs that count should yield a straight line (if this theory holds); any deviation would prompt either a refinement of K assignments or indicate new dynamics. Upcoming facilities like the Electron-Ion Collider or continued high-luminosity runs of LHC experiments could populate the mass spectrum of possible SAT-related states and thus offer a testing ground. Another domain is the **neutrino sector**: as measurements pin down the absolute neutrino masses and confirm the mass ordering (normal hierarchy, as current data hint【18†L91-L98】), theorists can attempt to fit those into the exponential scheme. If, say, neutrinos ended up having a ratio pattern that neatly fits exp(-σ ΔK) with a common ratio between ν₁–ν₂ and ν₂–ν₃, that would be striking (though presently, with only upper limits and mass-squared differences known, this is speculative). Conversely, if neutrino masses (once known) stubbornly resist any simple exponential fit regardless of what K one assigns, it may suggest this idea doesn’t apply to them – or requires additional new physics (like sterile neutrinos or ψ–τ couplings) to explain. Beyond the Standard Model, should a new spectrum of particles be discovered (for example, in a dark sector or a GUT-scale spectrum), researchers could check if those masses fall in geometric series, which might hint at an underlying topological structuring. Precision cosmology and astrophysics might also provide indirect clues: e.g., the pattern of scalar field masses or axion-like particle masses could exhibit exponential hierarchies that align with topological origins. On the theoretical side, the SAT team plans to “fix κ, σ, and ε… and convert scaling laws into absolute numbers” once the underlying geometry is solved【1†L103-L110】. When that happens, the mass predictions will become sharper – producing *forecast plots* of mass vs complexity that experiments can directly aim to confirm or refute. In preparation, one suggested action (per the evidence map) is to produce such plots for known sectors【18†L112-L120】. If those plots show a straight line for a given family and data points fall on it, that will be a huge validation; if not, adjustments or new ideas will be needed. In conclusion, the mass-from-topology proposal is still awaiting its crucial test. The next few years of accumulating particle data (especially in exotics and neutrinos) will either reveal a hidden regularity consistent with a geometric progression – thereby lending credence to SAT<sub>4D</sub> – or simply find masses where they are expected with no obvious geometric pattern, in which case this idea may remain more of a curious mathematical Ansatz unless new evidence emerges. In any event, ensuring compatibility with strict bounds (e.g. the neutrino masses【18†L91-L98】 and the non-observation of proton decay for GUT-scale masses【18†L83-L90】) will be mandatory: SAT<sub>4D</sub> must demonstrate that its topological mass mechanism can coexist with all known mass constraints while hopefully illuminating why those masses take the values they do.

Here’s the **Good News / Bad News** summary of where SAT<sub>4D</sub> predictions currently stand based on available experimental data:

---

## ✅ GOOD NEWS: SAT<sub>4D</sub> Still Stands — and Might Be Right

### θ₄-Defect Optics
- **No falsification yet.**
- Large-scale cosmic birefringence is ruled out, **but localized, achromatic phase steps (as SAT predicts) remain viable** — they just need to be rare or subtle.
- This means the prediction is **still testable** and hasn't been disproven.

### GW Polarization Fractions
- **No detection of scalar/vector GW modes — but SAT<sub>4D</sub> expects them to be small.**
- Current observational limits are **consistent with the SAT<sub>4D</sub> small-ε regime**.
- **Future improvements could either validate or constrain this further.**

### Exotic Hadron Widths
- **Perfect agreement.**
- All observed tetraquarks/pentaquarks have finite widths and short lifetimes.
- **No stable >3-quark states** have been found — exactly as SAT predicts.
- This is a **clear success** for SAT’s topological reconnection model.

### Mass Hierarchies
- **Consistent with trends.**
- Mass hierarchies in particle physics are real — and SAT’s exponential/topological suppression **could** explain them.
- No known particle mass outright contradicts the log-linear relation **if K-values are chosen sensibly.**

---

## ⚠️ BAD NEWS: Tensions, Limits, and Pending Risks

### θ₄-Defect Optics
- **Global phase steps (e.g. fixed Δφ ~ 0.24 rad everywhere) are ruled out.**
- SAT<sub>4D</sub> has to remain strictly in the "localized effects only" lane to survive.
- This means **defect density or coupling κ must be very small**, or it’ll get ruled out.

### GW Polarization Fractions
- If SAT had predicted **even 5–10% scalar/vector modes**, it would be **already falsified**.
- The fact that ε must be **≪ 1** for compatibility with observations could be seen as fine-tuned.
- So this prediction is **weaker** unless future detectors start to pick up sub-percent deviations.

### Exotic Hadron Widths
- **One exotic discovery with anomalously long lifetime would be fatal.**
- SAT<sub>4D</sub> rests on a sharp inequality: **higher-n exotics must not be more stable.**
- So far, all’s good — but if something like a quasi-stable hexaquark appears… it’s game over.

### Mass Hierarchies
- No obvious **geometric mass progression** has been seen in existing particles.
- The electron/muon/tau masses don’t fall in a perfect exponential chain.
- This doesn’t falsify the prediction (since SAT allows different σ, ΔK per family), but **it dilutes its testability**.

---

| Prediction Area         | Verdict                           | Testability |
